datasets.eval_protocol: Used as an OOD dataset for CIFAR-10-trained models; OOD detection is scored by AUROC using maximum predicted confidence. The split is not specified.

baselines.name: MART
baselines.fair_comparison: Discussed against other methods achieving around 57% robust accuracy; other matching conditions are not specified.

metrics.name: robust accuracy
metrics.caveat: Attack-based evaluations are upper bounds on true robust accuracy and can overestimate it when attacks fail; the paper reports AutoAttack results and, when available, the worst result across AutoAttack and other evaluations.

metrics.name: common-corruption accuracy
metrics.caveat: The aggregate averages across corruption types and severities; the paper also makes breakdowns by corruption and severity available.

metrics.name: expected calibration error (ECE)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports ECE both before and after temperature rescaling, along with the optimal rescaling temperature; rescaling reduces but does not completely eliminate the reported calibration gap.

metrics.name: relative standard deviation (RSD) of robust accuracy over classes
metrics.caveat: Lower RSD indicates more uniform classwise performance; the paper reports it alongside average robust accuracy.

metrics.name: membership inference accuracy
metrics.caveat: Inference accuracy may largely reflect the generalization gap rather than additional leakage from confidence; the paper compares it with a baseline determined by the generalization gap.

controls.name: standardly trained models
controls.detail: Used as an unmodified reference alongside robustly trained models in analyses including calibration, OOD detection, and privacy leakage.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether the reported pattern is also present in standardly trained models; it does not by itself isolate the effect of robust training from other training differences.

confounds.name: AutoAttack may overestimate robustness because its attacks fail on a model
confounds.detail: The headline robust-accuracy result could remain high even if a stronger or adaptive attack finds more adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper flags cases where Square Attack lowers robust accuracy by more than 0.2 percentage points relative to the white-box attacks, encourages adaptive evaluations, and reports additional evaluations when available. For Xiao et al.'s model, Square Attack with 30 random restarts reduced robust accuracy from 18.50% to 7.40%.

confounds.name: Privacy leakage attributed to robust training may instead reflect the generalization gap
confounds.detail: Membership inference accuracy could be elevated for reasons captured by the train–test generalization gap, without an additional effect of robust training.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares confidence-based membership inference accuracy with a baseline determined by the generalization gap and reports that confidence does not yield much higher inference accuracy than that baseline.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness or accuracy advantages may be due to extra training data
confounds.detail: Models trained with extra data may outperform others because of the additional data rather than the training technique being compared.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The leaderboard explicitly highlights models that use extra data, allowing this condition to be identified; the paper does not claim to eliminate this explanation.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates on the CIFAR-10 test set; reports accuracy under perturbation budget ε=8 for the defense evaluations. For PixelCNN detection, reports likelihood in bits/dimension and detection results at a threshold giving 1% false-positive rate. PixelDefend uses ε_defend=16 for its purification procedure.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates image-classification defenses at perturbation budget ε=2, reporting accuracy. For the stochastic padding-and-resizing defense, the paper uses 1,000 randomly selected images; it notes that the original evaluation instead used a subset correctly classified by every member of a fixed ensemble. Perturbation sizes ε are in pixel-intensity units with values in [0,255].

baselines.name: Undefended classifier
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with JPEG compression at quality 75 on ImageNet, using PGD-generated transfer attacks at ε=2; reported accuracies are 0% for the undefended model and 15% for JPEG compression.

baselines.name: JPEG compression (quality 75)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on ImageNet at ε=2; the paper reports transfer-attack accuracy alongside accuracy under an end-to-end SPSA attack.

baselines.name: PixelDefend
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 at ε=8; compares transfer-based FGSM evaluation with an end-to-end SPSA attack.

baselines.name: High-level Guided Denoiser
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on ImageNet at ε=2; compares the transfer-based evaluation using the undefended model as surrogate with an end-to-end PGD attack.

baselines.name: Stochastic padding-and-resizing defense (Xie et al.)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on ImageNet at ε=2; compares the ensemble-pattern transfer attack with an attack that optimizes the expected objective over the model's internal randomness.

baselines.name: Adversarially trained network (Madry et al.)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 at ε=8 against PGD and SPSA.

metrics.name: Accuracy / adversarial accuracy
metrics.caveat: Accuracy against a particular evaluation attack can overstate true adversarial robustness because the attack may fail to find adversarial examples; the paper evaluates with stronger or end-to-end attacks and reports the resulting accuracy.

metrics.name: Adversarial obscurity bound
metrics.caveat: It is only a lower bound on obscurity because the attack provides a lower bound on true adversarial risk, not an exact value; the paper reports the bound alongside evaluation accuracy.

metrics.name: PixelCNN likelihood (bits/dimension)
metrics.caveat: Low likelihood can flag oblivious adversarial examples, but an adaptive attacker can jointly optimize misclassification and likelihood; the paper reports detection performance for such adaptive examples too.

metrics.name: False-positive rate
metrics.caveat: A detector's false-positive rate alone does not show that it detects adaptive adversarial examples; the paper reports detection rate at the same threshold, including a threshold set to 1% false-positive rate.

metrics.name: Detection rate
metrics.caveat: Detection of adversarial examples generated without knowledge of the detector can be misleading; the paper also reports detection for examples optimized jointly for misclassification and likelihood.

controls.name: Undefended classifier reference
controls.detail: The paper reports the undefended ImageNet classifier alongside the JPEG-compressed classifier under the same PGD-generated transfer attack at ε=2.
controls.rules_out: That JPEG's higher accuracy in this comparison is simply the accuracy of the underlying undefended classifier.

confounds.name: Transfer-attack weakness due to surrogate mismatch
confounds.detail: A defense may appear robust because adversarial examples for the surrogate model do not transfer, even when the defended model itself has adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Attacks the end-to-end defended model directly: SPSA for non-differentiable JPEG and PixelDefend, PGD for the differentiable denoiser, and optimization over the stochastic model's expected objective.

confounds.name: Gradient masking in adversarially trained models
confounds.detail: The model could mask gradients during training, making gradient-based evaluation appear stronger than its true robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates the CIFAR-10 adversarially trained model with SPSA as well as PGD at ε=8; SPSA gives 51% accuracy, and succeeds when PGD does not on only 0.2% of images.

confounds.name: PixelCNN detection works only against attacks oblivious to the detector
confounds.detail: Adversarial examples may be detected when they have low likelihood, while examples optimized with knowledge of the detector may remain misclassified without being flagged.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Jointly optimizes misclassification and PixelCNN likelihood; at the threshold giving a 1% false-positive rate, the detector detects 0% of these adversarial examples.

confounds.name: Stochastic-defense transfer attack overfits to its fixed surrogate ensemble
confounds.detail: An attack on the 21 fixed padding-resize submodels may not represent an attack on the stochastic model itself.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Directly attacks the stochastic model's expected objective by sampling its random paddings and resizings during optimization.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses both a binary task (negative examples ‘1’, positive examples ‘3’) and a 10-class task. For the bound-tightness experiment, estimates expectations on the test dataset; trains 30 epochs with ε=0.1 and evaluates the inner maximization using a 20-iteration white-box FGSMk/PGD attack. For the 10-class λ experiment, trains 50 epochs with ε=0.1 and evaluates robust accuracy using 40-iteration white-box FGSMk/PGD with step size 0.005. In the defense comparisons, uses ε=0.3; evaluates with 40-iteration white-box FGSMk/PGD (step size 0.01), 1,000-iteration PGD, and C&W at ℓ2 distance 0.005. Black-box evaluation uses 40-iteration FGSMk with step size 0.01 and gradients from Natural or Madry source models. Reports natural and robust accuracy; split details are not stated.

datasets.name: CIFAR10
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 10-class classification with ResNet-18 for the λ experiment and WRN-34-10 for defense comparisons. For the λ experiment, trains 100 epochs with ε=0.031 and evaluates using 20-iteration white-box FGSMk/PGD with step size 0.003. Defense comparisons use ε=0.031 and evaluate with 20-iteration white-box FGSMk/PGD (step size 0.003), 1,000-iteration PGD, DeepFool, LBFGSAttack, MI-FGSM, and C&W. Black-box evaluation uses 20-iteration FGSMk with step size 0.003 and gradients from Natural or Madry source models. Reports natural and robust accuracy; split details are not stated.

datasets.name: Tiny ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated in the black-box NeurIPS 2018 Adversarial Vision Challenge. The competition dataset is described as 550,000 data points including data augmentation and 200 classes. Defenses return labels only and are attacked by the top-5 submissions in the untargeted attack track. Score is the smallest perturbation distance that causes an incorrect label; the paper reports mean ℓ2 perturbation distance. A split is not specified.

baselines.name: Natural (naturally trained model)
baselines.fair_comparison: For black-box MNIST and CIFAR10 comparisons, uses the same stated network architectures as the corresponding defense setup and evaluates under the same dataset-specific FGSMk attack settings; no other matching is stated.

baselines.name: Madry ([MMS+18])
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on MNIST and CIFAR10 under the same stated black-box FGSMk attack settings; the paper implements the method using the stated CNN and WRN-34-10 architectures. No further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [WSMK18] robust optimization defense
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison at ε=0.031 in ℓ∞; the table reports its FGSM20/PGD result. No further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [MMS+18] robust optimization defense
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same dataset and stated threat-model conditions in the relevant tables; CIFAR10 uses ε=0.031 in ℓ∞ and FGSM20/PGD, while MNIST uses ε=0.3 in ℓ∞ and FGSM40/PGD. No further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [ZSLG16] regularization method
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison at ε=0.031 in ℓ∞ under FGSM20/PGD. No further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [KGB17] regularization method
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison at ε=0.031 in ℓ∞ under FGSM20/PGD. No further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [RDV17] regularization method
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison at ε=0.031 in ℓ∞ under FGSM20/PGD. No further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [BRRG18] defense
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison under the [ACW18] evaluation results reported in the table; no further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [MLW+18] defense
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison under the [ACW18] evaluation results reported in the table; no further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [DAL+18] defense
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison under the [ACW18] evaluation results reported in the table; no further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [SKN+18] defense
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison under the [ACW18] evaluation results reported in the table; no further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [NKM17] defense
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 comparison under the [ACW18] evaluation results reported in the table; no further matching is stated.

baselines.name: [SKC18] defense
baselines.fair_comparison: MNIST comparison under the [ACW18] evaluation results reported in the table; no further matching is stated.

metrics.name: Robust accuracy
metrics.caveat: Robust-accuracy results can be misleading when defenses rely on obfuscated gradients or are evaluated with insufficient attacks; the paper reports results under stronger iterative and varied white-box attacks, and also black-box transfer attacks.

metrics.name: Mean ℓ2 perturbation distance to failure (Adversarial Vision Challenge score)

controls.name: Naturally trained, unmodified model
controls.detail: The paper trains Natural models without adversarial training and evaluates them alongside TRADES in black-box transfer attacks. It also uses natural training to estimate the optimal natural error and surrogate risk in the MNIST bound-tightness experiment.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against an unmodified reference shows whether the reported behavior differs from natural training; in the bound experiment it supplies the paper’s reference estimates for natural and surrogate risk.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness caused by obfuscated gradients or insufficient attack strength
confounds.detail: A defense could appear to have high robust accuracy because its gradients obstruct or weaken the tested attack, rather than because it withstands adversarial perturbations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates with long iterative FGSMk/PGD attacks and several different white-box attacks, including DeepFool, LBFGSAttack, MI-FGSM, and C&W, and also tests black-box FGSMk transfer attacks.

evidence_standards.name: Reported ± values for λ-sensitivity results
evidence_standards.detail: Table 4 reports natural and robust accuracy with ± values. The paper does not specify what the ± values represent, the number of runs or seeds, a statistical test, or a threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated under the l∞ threat model at ε=0.3. Deterministic-defense results use the whole test set; robust accuracy is the percentage of points for which the attack finds no adversarial example, with AutoAttack counting a point as non-robust if any component attack succeeds. Randomized-defense experiments are also reported, with statistics over 5 runs.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated under l∞ at ε=8/255 and ε=0.031, and l2 at ε=0.5; randomized-defense experiments additionally use l∞ ε=4/255. Deterministic-defense results use the whole test set. Randomized-defense results are averaged over 5 runs, except Yang et al., which uses 1000 test points. Robust accuracy counts a point as non-robust if any AutoAttack component finds an adversarial example.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated under the l∞ threat model at ε=8/255. Uses the whole test set; robust accuracy counts a point as non-robust if any AutoAttack component finds an adversarial example.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated under l∞ at ε=4/255 and l2 at ε=3, using 1000 points from the validation set. Robust accuracy counts a point as non-robust if any AutoAttack component finds an adversarial example.

baselines.name: PGD
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with APGD on the same robust MNIST and CIFAR-10 models and test points; the paper varies PGD step sizes and iteration budgets. In the loss comparison, PGD uses three step sizes: ε/10, ε/4, and 2ε.

baselines.name: PGD with Momentum
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with APGD on the same robust MNIST and CIFAR-10 models and test points. The step-size comparison uses 1000 iterations and step sizes ε/t for t∈{0.5,1,2,4,10,25,100}; the loss comparison uses the same three step sizes as PGD.

baselines.name: Original-paper reported robust accuracy
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the evaluated defense models at the threat-model ε used in the original paper. The authors note that some original-paper statistics use test-set subsets, so the evaluation samples are not always matched.

metrics.name: Robust accuracy
metrics.caveat: An attack that fails to find adversarial examples can overestimate robustness; the paper reports individual-attack results and AutoAttack's worst-case combination, counting success by any component.

metrics.name: Cross-entropy loss
metrics.caveat: Its gradients can vanish when logits are strongly scaled, making PGD ineffective; the paper also evaluates with the scale- and shift-invariant DLR loss and measures the fraction of zero gradient entries in a logit-rescaling experiment.

metrics.name: Difference of Logits Ratio (DLR) loss
metrics.caveat: The paper introduces it to avoid CE's logit-scale sensitivity and compares it with CE and CW; it reports that CW can be substantially worse than DLR and that DLR has less severe failure cases.

metrics.name: Carlini-Wagner (CW) loss
metrics.caveat: It is not invariant to logit rescaling; the paper compares it with the scale-invariant DLR loss.

confounds.name: PGD may appear weak because its fixed step size is suboptimal or its budget is poorly used
confounds.detail: An apparent robustness result could reflect attack optimization failure rather than actual resistance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare APGD against PGD with Momentum across fixed step sizes and iteration budgets on the same models and test points; APGD achieves higher CE loss and generally lower robust accuracy.

confounds.name: Gradient masking or loss-induced vanishing gradients
confounds.detail: A defense could appear robust because the attack's loss gradients fail, rather than because the classifier resists adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure zero entries in gradients and PGD robust accuracy while rescaling logits in the CIFAR-10 model; also evaluate with DLR and combine gradient-based attacks with FAB and gradient-free Square Attack.

confounds.name: Attack-specific failures could make an individual attack's robustness estimate misleading
confounds.detail: A high robust accuracy from one attack may reflect that attack failing on the model or on particular inputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report each component attack and AutoAttack's worst-case result across APGD, FAB, and Square Attack; the paper notes that different attacks can succeed on different points.

confounds.name: Randomness in a defense could make a single-run robustness result unstable
confounds.detail: The same input can receive different decisions across runs, so a single attack run could misstate robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For randomized defenses, report statistics over 5 runs; use 20 gradient computations per APGD update and accept Square Attack updates based on average target loss over 20 forward passes.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated-run reporting for randomized defenses
evidence_standards.detail: Report mean and standard deviation over 5 runs for clean accuracy and AutoAttack robust accuracy. No statistical test or numerical margin for declaring a difference real is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed AutoAttack evaluation budget
evidence_standards.detail: For deterministic evaluations, use 100 iterations for each white-box attack, 9 target classes for targeted APGD and FAB, and one 5000-query Square Attack run. The paper does not specify a statistical significance threshold for differences.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Compare dπ for test images and adversarial examples; the manifold-distance analysis uses successful ℓ2-bounded attacks maximizing XEnt. Also used for gradient visualizations; further evaluation settings are referred to the appendix.

datasets.name: FMNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Compare dπ for test images and adversarial examples; the manifold-distance analysis uses successful ℓ2-bounded attacks maximizing XEnt. Also used for gradient visualizations; further evaluation settings are referred to the appendix.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for the manifold-distance and gradient-visualization experiments. For ROAR/KAR, replace the most-important or least-important pixels at fractions 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, and 0.9 with a constant, retrain CNNs on the modified data, and measure test accuracy; the reported accuracy is averaged over three CNNs per attribution method and fraction.

datasets.name: 2-dimensional toy dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Points from two distinct bivariate Gaussian distributions are classified by three two-layer ReLU networks: one trained on original data and two trained against weak and strong adversaries. Compare decision boundaries and adversarial-example distributions.

baselines.name: Standard-trained DNN/CNN
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper describes standard and adversarially trained networks of the same architecture.

baselines.name: Random attribution (g_Rand)
baselines.fair_comparison: Assign random attribution values to input features; use its ROAR AOC or KAR AUC as the reference subtracted from the corresponding attribution score.

controls.name: Standard-trained reference network
controls.detail: Compare adversarially trained networks with networks trained on natural images; the paper specifies the same architecture for the standard and adversarially trained families.
controls.rules_out: That the reported differences are simply properties of the architecture rather than the adversarial-training condition.

controls.name: Random attribution (g_Rand)
controls.detail: Use random feature-attribution values as the reference for ROAR and KAR, subtracting its curve area from the evaluated attribution method’s curve area.
controls.rules_out: That the ROAR/KAR score reflects no more than the reference performance of random feature ordering.

confounds.name: Visually sharp gradients may not accurately reflect the DNN’s internal representation
confounds.detail: A gradient can look interpretable to a human without being an accurate account of the features used by the network.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate gradients quantitatively with ROAR and KAR: occlude features according to attribution rankings, retrain on the modified data, and measure test-accuracy changes.

confounds.name: Apparent manifold proximity may result from attacks that failed to change the prediction
confounds.detail: Failed attacks may be zero matrices because of loss-function saturation, which could make their distance to the image manifold misleadingly small.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Remove attacks that fail to change the prediction from the manifold-distance analysis.

evidence_standards.name: Three CNNs per attribution method and occlusion fraction
evidence_standards.detail: Report test accuracy as the average over three CNNs for each fraction in the ROAR/KAR evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: Report linear and Spearman rank correlations
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports both correlation coefficients for the relationships shown; it does not specify a significance test or threshold for declaring a difference real.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the full 10K-image test set at epsilon=8/255. Report nominal accuracy and adversarial accuracy under FGSM-20, Untargeted, and Multi-Targeted attacks; use adversarial accuracy (test-set accuracy after the attack) for the latter attacks. The attack losses use differences between logits. The paper specifies softplus activations for its CIFAR-10 models; no input preprocessing is stated.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the first 1K test images at epsilon=4/255 and epsilon=16/255. Report nominal accuracy, adversarial accuracy under Untargeted attack, and Random-Targeted attack success rate (whether the randomly selected target label is output). The attack losses use differences between logits. Multi-Targeted evaluation is omitted because looping over 1,000 labels is computationally expensive. The paper specifies ResNet-152 with softplus activations; no input preprocessing is stated.

baselines.name: Adversarial training (ADV)
baselines.fair_comparison: For CIFAR-10, recreated comparisons use the same network architecture and activation function as the LLR models. For ImageNet at epsilon=4/255, the recreated comparison uses ResNet-152 and softplus. At epsilon=16/255, the comparison uses published models; no matched setup is stated.

baselines.name: TRADES
baselines.fair_comparison: For CIFAR-10, recreated comparisons use the same network architecture and activation function as the LLR models. The published TRADES model uses Wide-ResNet-34-10 and is reported separately, not in the main table. No ImageNet comparison is reported.

baselines.name: CURE
baselines.fair_comparison: For CIFAR-10, recreated comparisons use the same network architecture and activation function as the LLR models. No ImageNet comparison is reported.

baselines.name: Denoising model (DENOISE)
baselines.fair_comparison: For ImageNet at epsilon=4/255, the comparison is a recreated model using ResNet-152 and softplus. At epsilon=16/255, the comparison uses a published model; no matched setup is stated.

metrics.name: Adversarial accuracy
metrics.caveat: Accuracy can depend on attack strength, and weak attacks may overstate robustness when gradient obfuscation is present. The paper reports results under multiple attack strengths and includes Untargeted and Multi-Targeted attacks where feasible.

metrics.name: Random-Targeted attack success rate
metrics.caveat: This measures whether the randomly chosen target label becomes the output, rather than overall accuracy; the paper reports it alongside adversarial accuracy, especially for ImageNet at epsilon=16/255.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness is due to gradient obfuscation or an underpowered attack
confounds.detail: A model could appear robust because a weak gradient-based attack fails to find adversarial examples, rather than because the model is genuinely robust.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate with stronger attacks, including Untargeted and Multi-Targeted attacks on CIFAR-10, and tune attack loss and optimization to obtain the lowest adversarial accuracy. Also compare accuracy as attack strength increases and inspect loss-surface plots and gamma(epsilon,x) measurements.

confounds.name: Robustness at epsilon=16/255 may not represent robustness to imperceptible perturbations
confounds.detail: The reported robustness could concern perturbations large enough to be perceptible, rather than the kind of imperceptible adversarial changes motivating the robustness claim.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors inspect generated images, observe super-imposed object parts, and explicitly state that the perturbation radius may be too large for the robustness problem.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates on the test set using test accuracy under adversarial attacks. Training adversaries use PGD with ε_train=0.3, step size ε_train/4, and 10 iterations. The EOT-PGD robustness curves use n=20 gradient samples per iteration and 20 attack iterations across perturbation bounds; the supplementary EOT-PGD tables also report n=5, 10, and 20. Randomized-network ensemble inference uses 20 sample models.

datasets.name: CIFAR10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates on the test set using test accuracy under adversarial attacks, including the combined-attack robust accuracy. Training adversaries use PGD with ε_train=8/255, step size ε_train/4, and 10 iterations. The main attack table uses ε=8/255 and 50 PGD iterations; EOT attacks use n=10 sample models per iteration. Randomized-network ensemble inference uses 20 sample models.

datasets.name: STL10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates on the test set using test accuracy under adversarial attacks. Training adversaries use PGD with ε_train=0.03, step size ε_train/4, and 10 iterations. EOT-PGD robustness curves use n=20 gradient samples per iteration and 20 attack iterations across perturbation bounds; supplementary tables also report n=5, 10, and 20. Randomized-network ensemble inference uses 20 sample models.

baselines.name: Adv-BNN
baselines.fair_comparison: GradDiv is applied to Adv-BNN and compared with the same randomized-network baseline under the same dataset and attack evaluations; Adv-BNN hyperparameters are set to α_KL=0.02 and prior standard deviation 0.05, 0.1, and 0.15 for MNIST, CIFAR10, and STL10, respectively.

baselines.name: Adversarial Training (Adv.train)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same datasets and attack evaluations; no additional matching or tuning procedure is specified.

baselines.name: Random Self-Ensemble (RSE)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same datasets and attack evaluations; no additional matching or tuning procedure is specified.

baselines.name: Parametric Noise Injection (PNI)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the CIFAR10 attack evaluation; no additional matching or tuning procedure is specified.

baselines.name: Mixup Inference (MI)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the CIFAR10 attack evaluation; no additional matching or tuning procedure is specified.

baselines.name: No defense
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same datasets and attack evaluations; described as a standard deterministic network trained on clean training images.

metrics.name: Test accuracy
metrics.caveat: The authors note that evaluation against a finite set of attacks cannot guarantee that no stronger adaptive attack exists; they therefore evaluate against a diverse set of attacks and include EOT attacks.

metrics.name: Total robust accuracy
metrics.caveat: Reported as accuracy against the combined attacks; the authors caution that finite attack evaluations cannot establish robustness to every possible stronger adaptive attack.

metrics.name: Mean cosine similarity between gradient samples
Transferability between sample models
metrics.caveat: Reported as target test accuracy for source-to-target transfer attacks; higher accuracy indicates lower transferability.

controls.name: Adv-BNN without GradDiv
controls.detail: The unregularized Adv-BNN baseline is compared with Adv-BNN trained using GradDiv.
controls.rules_out: A difference supports an effect from adding GradDiv to the baseline rather than merely using the randomized Adv-BNN model.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness is caused by obfuscated gradients rather than genuine resistance
confounds.detail: A defense with obfuscated gradients can appear robust under some attacks while remaining vulnerable to stronger or black-box attacks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper checks whether one-step attacks outperform iterative attacks, whether black-box attacks outperform white-box attacks, whether unbounded attacks fail to reach 100% success, whether random sampling finds adversarial examples, and whether increasing distortion fails to increase attack success. It reports the corresponding attack comparisons, Square-attack results, distortion curves, and a random search with 10^5 samples.

confounds.name: A stronger adaptive attack could still break the defense
confounds.detail: Robustness on the evaluated finite attack suite could occur even if an unevaluated stronger adaptive attack succeeds.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors explicitly acknowledge that finite empirical evaluation cannot guarantee the non-existence of a stronger adaptive attack; they evaluate a diverse set of state-of-the-art attacks, including EOT variants.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and standard deviation for stochastic-defense test accuracy
evidence_standards.detail: Tables report mean ± standard deviation for stochastic defenses; the number of runs or seeds and any statistical significance test are not specified.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: ImageNet validation set; reports clean top-1 accuracy and top-1 accuracy against PGD-200 with maximum perturbation ε=4 and step size β=1. The paper reports that robustness converges by 200 iterations.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates adversarially trained ResNet-18 models with AutoAttack; the evaluation split is not specified. Training uses PGD-1 with ε=8 and β=8.

baselines.name: ReLU adversarial training (standard adversarial training)
baselines.fair_comparison: For the ResNet-50 comparisons, uses the same stated training setup, changing the activation/gradient condition under study.

baselines.name: Standard training
baselines.fair_comparison: The EfficientNet-L1 standard-training accuracy is compared with SAT using the stated EfficientNet training setup.

metrics.name: Adversarial robustness (top-1 accuracy under attack)
metrics.caveat: A weak or misdirected attack can overstate robustness, including through gradient masking; the paper reports PGD-200 on ImageNet and runs attack-iteration and perturbation-size sanity tests, and uses AutoAttack on CIFAR-10.

controls.name: ReLU adversarial-training reference
controls.detail: The unmodified ReLU condition is run alongside smooth-activation conditions under the stated ResNet-50 training setup.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether the smooth-activation condition changes accuracy or robustness.

controls.name: Attacker-only and optimizer-only gradient ablations
controls.detail: Use Parametric Softplus gradients only for crafting training adversarial examples, or only for network parameter updates, while retaining ReLU in the forward pass; compare with the ReLU condition and the condition improving both gradients.
controls.rules_out: Separates the contribution of better attacker gradients from better optimizer gradients and tests whether both are needed for the combined result.

controls.name: SmoothReLU
controls.detail: Smooths ReLU only for x≥0 and remains zero for x<0; compared with ReLU under adversarial training.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the gains require nonzero responses to negative inputs, rather than smoothness.

controls.name: PGD-2 training
controls.detail: Compared with the PGD-1 ReLU baseline, using more attack iterations and twice the attacker cost.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the effect attributed to improved gradients can instead be obtained simply by spending more computation on the training attacker.

controls.name: 200-epoch training
controls.detail: Compared with the default 100-epoch schedule.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether longer training alone accounts for the gains associated with improved gradients.

controls.name: ELU versus CELU across α values
controls.detail: Compares non-smooth ELU and smooth CELU over α values from 1.0 to 2.0.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether robustness changes track smoothness rather than the choice of α alone.

controls.name: Scaled standard adversarial training
controls.detail: Compares standard adversarial training and SAT on scaled ResNet-family models, including ResNeXt-152-32x8d at resolution 380.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether SAT's scaling results can be explained by network scaling alone.

confounds.name: Gains come from nonzero responses to negative inputs, not smoothness
confounds.detail: The smooth activations considered initially respond to x<0, so that property could explain their advantage over ReLU.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper trains with SmoothReLU, which is smooth but remains zero for x<0; it reports +7.3 percentage points robustness and +0.6 accuracy versus ReLU.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness is caused by gradient masking or an insufficient attack
confounds.detail: A failing or insufficiently optimized attacker could make measured robustness look high without the model being robust.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On ImageNet, robustness decreases as PGD iterations rise from 5 to 10 to 50 and converges at PGD-200; increasing ε from 4 to 8 lowers robustness by more than 25%, and ε=16 circumvents the model. The paper also visualizes loss landscapes and uses AutoAttack on CIFAR-10.

confounds.name: The gains are just a consequence of more attack computation or longer training
confounds.detail: Harder training examples from additional attack iterations, or lower loss from a longer schedule, could explain the observed performance changes without the claimed gradient-quality effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper tests PGD-2 and a 200-epoch schedule: PGD-2 gives a small robustness gain with an accuracy decrease, while longer training gains accuracy but loses robustness; these do not reproduce the joint improvement reported with better optimizer gradients.

confounds.name: Scaling network capacity, rather than smooth activation training, explains the robustness gains
confounds.detail: Larger or higher-resolution networks can improve adversarial-training results independently of SAT.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares scaled standard adversarial training with SAT; for the compound ResNeXt-152-32x8d at resolution 380, it reports 46.3% robustness for standard adversarial training versus 51.2% for SAT.

confounds.name: The prior-art advantage isolates SAT itself
confounds.detail: The headline comparison changes both the activation and architecture: EfficientNet-L1 with SILU is compared with prior art [49], and the paper says the improvement mainly stems from both the activation and the stronger architecture.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by the prior-art comparison; the paper explicitly attributes the difference to both factors.

evidence_standards.name: PGD attack-convergence check on ImageNet
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports robustness under PGD-200 after checking PGD-5, PGD-10, PGD-50, and PGD-200; the reported values are 48.7%, 43.7%, 42.7%, and 42.3%, respectively, with the evaluation described as converged at 200 iterations.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Train and evaluate on CIFAR-10; the paper does not specify a split beyond training and test data. Images are normalized to [0,1]. It reports natural test accuracy and adversarial test accuracy under FGSM, PGD-20, PGD-100, and C&W∞ (the L∞ version of C&W optimized by PGD-30). In the perturbation-bound experiments, test ε is 8/255 and also 16/255; PGD attacks use random starts and step size 2/255. The WRN evaluations use the evaluation protocol of DAT or TRADES, respectively.

datasets.name: SVHN
datasets.eval_protocol: Train and evaluate on SVHN; the paper does not specify a split beyond training and test data. Images are normalized to [0,1]. It reports natural test accuracy and adversarial test accuracy under FGSM, PGD-20, PGD-100, and C&W∞ (the L∞ version of C&W optimized by PGD-30). In the perturbation-bound experiments, test ε is 4/255 and also 8/255; PGD attacks use random starts and step size 2/255.

baselines.name: standard adversarial training (Madry)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 and SVHN with ResNet-18 across training perturbation bounds; the paper also reports a CIFAR-10 WRN-32-10 comparison using the same evaluations as FAT.

baselines.name: CAT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with FAT on CIFAR-10 using WRN-32-10 and the same evaluations; CAT results are reported from Wang et al. (2019).

baselines.name: DAT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with FAT on CIFAR-10 using WRN-32-10 and the same evaluations; DAT results are reported from Wang et al. (2019).

baselines.name: TRADES
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with FAT for TRADES on CIFAR-10 using WRN-34-10; the paper says performance evaluations are done exactly as in TRADES (Zhang et al., 2019b).

metrics.name: average backward propagations (BPs) for generating adversarial data

controls.name: standard adversarial training (PGD-K; τ=K)
controls.detail: The paper identifies conventional standard adversarial training as the special case of FAT with τ=K, removing early stopping.
controls.rules_out: A performance difference against this condition supports an effect from the friendly early-stopping mechanism rather than adversarial training alone.

controls.name: PGD-20 adversarial variants
controls.detail: For the CIFAR-10 two-class Small CNN representation visualization, compared with PGD-20-0 variants after natural-data warm-up; layer 7 outputs are visualized with PCA.
controls.rules_out: A difference in class mixing supports the claim that early stopping, rather than merely adding adversarial variants, reduces cross-over mixing.

evidence_standards.name: 5 repeated trials; median and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: For the τ experiments in Figure 4, the paper reports median test accuracy over five repeated adversarial-training trials and shows standard deviation as shaded color. It states no statistical test or numerical threshold for deciding that a difference is real.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports standard accuracy, PGD accuracy at ε=0.1 and ε=0.3, and exact verified robustness at ε=0.1. The PGD training adversary for the ε=0.3 models uses 40 iterations with step size 0.01. No evaluation split or evaluation-attack settings are specified.

datasets.name: CIFAR10
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports standard accuracy and robust accuracy at ε=8/255, including accuracy under PGD evaluation with 10 random restarts and 50 iterations. Training-time comparisons report time to reach 45% robust accuracy. No evaluation split is specified.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports standard top-1 accuracy and PGD robust accuracy at ε=2/255 and ε=4/255, with results for both one and 10 random restarts. The paper states that its evaluation PGD adversaries use 50 iterations; no evaluation split is specified.

baselines.name: PGD adversarial training (including PGD-7)
baselines.fair_comparison: On MNIST, both training methods use the same stated architecture and ε=0.3. On CIFAR10, the paper reruns publicly available PGD-7 training code on its hardware and compares time to the same 45% robust-accuracy threshold; the cited Madry result in Table 1 uses a different architecture.

baselines.name: Free adversarial training (m=8 on CIFAR10; m=4 on ImageNet)
baselines.fair_comparison: CIFAR10 runtime comparisons use the public training code rerun on the paper's hardware and compare time to 45% robust accuracy. ImageNet comparisons report both methods at the same ε values and include PGD results with one and 10 restarts. The cited CIFAR10 result from Shafahi et al. in Table 1 uses a different architecture.

metrics.name: PGD robust accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper warns that weak attacks can give a misleading sense of robustness; it evaluates with 50 PGD iterations and 10 random restarts, and also reports exact verification for small MNIST models.

metrics.name: Verified robustness (verified accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Exact verification is reported only at ε=0.1 for MNIST; verification at ε=0.3 was not feasible, and models on larger datasets rely on empirical tests.

controls.name: FGSM with zero initialization
controls.detail: Uses a zero-initialized perturbation instead of the main method's random initialization.
controls.rules_out: A comparison against this condition tests whether random initialization, rather than FGSM training alone, is needed for the reported robustness.

controls.name: FGSM with previous-minibatch initialization
controls.detail: Initializes each perturbation from the previous minibatch's perturbation rather than a uniformly random perturbation.
controls.rules_out: Its comparable robustness to random initialization supports the paper's claim that a nonzero initialization matters, rather than randomness specifically.

controls.name: FGSM with alternative step sizes
controls.detail: The paper compares α=ε, α=10/255, and α=16/255 for CIFAR10 at ε=8/255.
controls.rules_out: These comparisons test whether the result depends on the FGSM step size; the paper reports improved robustness at 10/255 and catastrophic overfitting at 16/255.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness is an artifact of a weak evaluation attack
confounds.detail: A model could appear robust to a weak attack without being robust to stronger adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates with PGD using 50 iterations and 10 random restarts; for small MNIST models, also reports exact MILP verification at ε=0.1.

confounds.name: The benefit comes from any nonzero starting perturbation, not specifically random initialization
confounds.detail: The headline result for random-initialized FGSM could be explained by starting away from zero, with the particular random initialization playing no special role.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares random initialization with previous-minibatch initialization and finds both yield robustness, with random initialization slightly better in the reported CIFAR10 comparison.

confounds.name: FGSM training can catastrophically overfit and lose robustness
confounds.detail: A training run may appear successful or be judged by its training setup even though PGD robustness suddenly collapses to zero.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures PGD accuracy during training on a small minibatch of training data and describes early stopping as a way to recover some failed runs.

evidence_standards.name: Three independent runs for the CIFAR10 epoch-sweep results
evidence_standards.detail: Figure 2 plots average model performance over 3 independent runs. The paper does not state a variance estimate, statistical test, or numerical margin for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: For 5×5 patches, validation results use 5,000 images and final results use a separate 5,000-image test set; additional validation curves examine other patch sizes. Certified accuracy is the fraction correctly classified and certified robust to the specified patch size. Ablated pixels are replaced by a specially encoded NULL value using additional input channels, as in [16].

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: For 5×5 patches, validation results use 5,000 images and final results use a separate 5,000-image test set; validation curves also examine patch sizes up to 9×9. Certified accuracy is the fraction correctly classified and certified robust to the specified patch size. Empirical attack evaluation uses 500 test images: patch IFGSM uses 80 random starts, 150 iterations per start, and step size 0.05; L∞ IFGSM uses 50 iterations and step size 0.5/255. Ablated pixels are replaced by a specially encoded NULL value using additional input channels, as in [16].

datasets.name: ImageNet-1000 (ILSVRC2012)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 42×42 patches using column smoothing with column width s=25. Uses 1,000 images for validation and a separate 1,000 for test; evaluates θ in {0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4}, selects θ=0.2 on validation, and reports test results. Certified accuracy is the fraction correctly classified and certified robust to the specified patch size. Ablated pixels are replaced by a specially encoded NULL value using additional input channels, as in [16].

baselines.name: Chiang et al. [9] interval bound propagation patch-certification method
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares reported certified and clean accuracies, using each technique's parameters for its highest certified accuracy; it does not state that the base models or training setups were matched.

baselines.name: Sparse randomized ablation / L₀ randomized smoothing [16]
Randomized column smoothing (randomized structured ablation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on MNIST and CIFAR-10 for 5×5 patches against derandomized column smoothing, with results shown for top-1 and thresholded variants; the optimal column width s is reported separately for each method.

baselines.name: Unprotected baseline model
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with column smoothing on the 500 CIFAR-10 test images used for empirical attack evaluation; the paper does not specify further matching details.

metrics.name: Certified accuracy
metrics.caveat: A robustness guarantee is not a guarantee of correctness and applies to the specified patch threat model, not general adversarial attacks; the paper reports clean accuracy alongside it and also evaluates empirical attacks.

metrics.name: Empirical accuracy under patch IFGSM attack

controls.name: Top-1-only column smoothing (no thresholding or abstention)
controls.detail: Uses the top-one class instead of allowing the base classifier to abstain or vote for multiple classes.
controls.rules_out: Comparing it with the thresholded version tests whether the reported result depends on thresholding and abstention.

controls.name: Randomized column smoothing
controls.detail: Uses randomized structured column ablations rather than exactly evaluating all possible column ablations.
controls.rules_out: Comparing it with derandomized column smoothing tests whether the gain is attributable to derandomization rather than merely using column ablation.

controls.name: Unprotected baseline model
controls.detail: An undefended model is evaluated alongside column smoothing on CIFAR-10 under patch and L∞ attacks.
controls.rules_out: The comparison shows whether the defended model's empirical attack performance differs from an unprotected reference.

confounds.name: The certified-accuracy gain comes from thresholding and abstention, rather than derandomization
confounds.detail: If thresholding alone explained the gain, the improvement would not persist when comparing randomized and derandomized column smoothing without thresholding.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares randomized column smoothing with both derandomized top-1 and thresholded variants on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and reports that derandomization improves certificates independently of thresholding.

confounds.name: The defense is especially vulnerable to general, non-patch attacks
confounds.detail: Because an L∞ attack affects all base classifiers simultaneously, the patch robustness guarantee does not apply and the defended model might be unusually vulnerable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates L∞-bounded IFGSM on CIFAR-10 and compares accuracy with an unprotected baseline; the paper reports a reduction but says it is not dramatic.

evidence_standards.name: Exact enumeration for certificates
evidence_standards.detail: The method evaluates all possible block or column ablations and counts class votes, yielding deterministic certificates rather than Monte Carlo estimates. The paper reports no seed aggregation, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests.

evidence_standards.name: Validation-based hyperparameter selection followed by separate test evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: For the reported MNIST and CIFAR-10 results, validation and test sets are separate; for ImageNet, θ is selected on 1,000 validation images and results are reported on 1,000 test images.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Validation accuracy on natural images and under ℓ∞-bounded attacks (ε=8): PGD-20, PGD-100, CW-100, and 10-restart PGD-20. The authors also report five trials for Free-m=8, including robustness against 20-random-restart PGD-20. No preprocessing is specified.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Validation accuracy on natural images and under ℓ∞-bounded PGD-20 and PGD-100 attacks (ε=8). No preprocessing is specified.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Validation top-1 accuracy on natural images and under non-targeted ℓ∞-bounded PGD attacks. For ε=2, report PGD-10/50/100 with step size 1; additional experiments use ε=4 and report PGD-10/50/100. Training batch size is 256. No preprocessing is specified.

baselines.name: Natural training
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as the unmodified reference; CIFAR natural models use Wide-ResNet 32-10. No further matching details are stated.

baselines.name: 7-PGD adversarially trained CIFAR-10 model (Madry et al., 2017; “adv_trained” checkpoint)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Free models using Wide-ResNet 32-10; the paper says it uses the standard hyperparameters from Madry et al. (2017).

baselines.name: Madry et al. 2-PGD adversarially trained CIFAR-100 model
baselines.fair_comparison: The authors train their own Wide-ResNet 32-10 model using the Madry et al. adversarial-training code.

baselines.name: Madry et al. 7-PGD adversarially trained CIFAR-100 model
baselines.fair_comparison: The authors train their own Wide-ResNet 32-10 model using the Madry et al. adversarial-training code.

baselines.name: YOPO 5-3
baselines.fair_comparison: For a direct comparison, the authors train Free on WRN-34-10 with batch size 256, matching the architecture and batch size used for the cited YOPO result.

baselines.name: 2-PGD adversarially trained ResNet-50
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Free-m=4 ResNet-50; both are trained against ℓ∞ ε=4 attacks, and all other hyperparameters are stated to be identical.

metrics.name: Natural-image validation accuracy
metrics.caveat: Increasing replay m can reduce clean accuracy; the paper reports robustness accuracy alongside it and discusses the tradeoff.

metrics.name: Accuracy under adversarial attacks (robust accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Results can depend on attack strength. The paper reports results at multiple PGD iteration counts and, for CIFAR-10, across attack losses and restart settings; it also reports that increasing ImageNet PGD from 50 to 100 steps did not meaningfully reduce accuracy.

controls.name: Natural training
controls.detail: Train the same task without adversarial training; natural-training models are reported alongside Free models.
controls.rules_out: That the reported robustness is already achieved by ordinary natural training.

confounds.name: Gradient masking rather than genuine robustness
confounds.detail: A model could appear robust to gradient-based attacks because its loss surface masks or obscures useful gradients, without actually resisting adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare Free-m=8 with 7-PGD training using projected cross-entropy loss surfaces along random and adversarial directions; the adversarial direction produces the largest loss change. Also evaluate with stronger PGD iterations, restarts, and CW attacks on CIFAR-10.

confounds.name: Mini-batch replay harms clean generalization or causes forgetting
confounds.detail: Repeatedly training on the same minibatch could reduce natural-image performance or cause catastrophic forgetting, rather than providing a cost-free route to useful robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure clean validation accuracy across replay values, including the natural-training reference; the paper reports the clean-accuracy changes alongside robustness results.

evidence_standards.name: Five trials for Free-m=8 on CIFAR-10
evidence_standards.detail: The authors say results are insensitive to initialization and report natural accuracy 85.95 ± 0.14 and 20-random-restart PGD-20 accuracy 46.49 ± 0.19. The paper does not specify a statistical test or a threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated under ℓ∞ and ℓ2 perturbations. For each example and attack magnitude, use 50 randomly initialized white-box PGD attacks per model and 50×(m−1) transfer attacks from the other models; an example is non-robust if any attack succeeds. The reported combined attack counts are 900 for MNIST-ℓ∞ and 1200 for MNIST-ℓ2. Reports clean accuracy and robust accuracy at multiple magnitudes; the excerpt does not specify the split size.

datasets.name: CIFAR10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated under ℓ∞ and ℓ2 perturbations. For each example and attack magnitude, use 10 randomly initialized white-box PGD attacks per model and 10×(m−1) transfer attacks from the other models; an example is non-robust if any attack succeeds. The reported combined attack counts are 320 for CIFAR10-ℓ∞ and 260 for CIFAR10-ℓ2. Reports clean accuracy and robust accuracy at multiple magnitudes; the excerpt does not specify the split size.

baselines.name: PGD-ε (standard fixed-magnitude adversarial training)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with MMA across perturbation magnitudes using the same combined white-box and transfer PGD evaluation protocol for each dataset-norm setting.

baselines.name: PGDLS-ε (PGD training with linear scaling of ε)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with MMA across perturbation magnitudes using the same combined white-box and transfer PGD evaluation protocol for each dataset-norm setting.

baselines.name: PGD-ens
baselines.fair_comparison: Ensemble of PGD-trained models with different ε values; evaluated alongside MMA under the same reported attack protocol. Predictions use majority vote, with softmax scores as the tie-breaker.

baselines.name: PGDLS-ens
baselines.fair_comparison: Ensemble of PGDLS-trained models with different ε values; evaluated alongside MMA under the same reported attack protocol. Predictions use majority vote, with softmax scores as the tie-breaker.

baselines.name: TRADES
baselines.fair_comparison: The authors compare MMA-32 with downloaded TRADES models selected because their clean accuracies are similar, and evaluate them under the same reported attacks.

metrics.name: RobAcc (robust accuracy under attack)
metrics.caveat: For ensembles, the authors caution that white-box PGD attacks may not be sufficiently effective; attacks on ensembles are described as relatively unexplored.

metrics.name: Training-point margin distribution
metrics.caveat: Margins are approximated using the norm of a 1000-step DDN attack; the authors note that solving for the shortest successful perturbation is non-convex and optimality cannot be guaranteed in practice.

controls.name: OMMA-32 (MMA objective without the additional clean-loss term)
controls.detail: Compared with MMA-32, which adds clean loss to the MMA objective; the paper visualizes input-space loss curves for both conditions using 50 training and 50 test examples, failed PGD perturbations at ε=8/255, and nine interpolated points.
controls.rules_out: A difference in loss-landscape steepness being attributable to the MMA margin objective alone; the comparison supports the role of the added clean-loss term in making the landscape steeper and PGD more effective at finding perturbations.

confounds.name: Gradient obfuscation makes PGD appear less successful than it is
confounds.detail: The reported robustness could reflect failure of gradient-based PGD rather than genuine resistance to adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: As a sanity check, run gradient-free SPSA on the first 100 test examples for all ℓ∞-MMA models; SPSA does not find successful adversarial examples on cases where PGD did not.

confounds.name: A flat input-space loss landscape weakens the training attack and leads to poor approximation of the shortest successful perturbation
confounds.detail: MMA’s apparent behavior or performance could be affected by AN-PGD failing to find an effective perturbation because the loss landscape is too flat.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Plot logit-margin losses along interpolations from clean examples to failed PGD perturbations for 50 training and 50 test examples; compare OMMA-32, PGD-8, and MMA-32, and show that adding clean loss makes most MMA loss curves more tilted.

confounds.name: The ensemble comparison may favor MMA because PGD attacks on ensembles are insufficiently effective
confounds.detail: MMA’s apparent advantage over PGD ensembles could be larger than the true difference if the ensemble attacks fail to find adversarial examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors explicitly caution that their white-box PGD attacks on ensembles may not be sufficiently effective.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Compares standard accuracy as training-set size varies for models trained against an ℓ2-bounded adversary; corresponding ℓ∞ results are in Appendix G. Also examines linear classifiers and feature restriction. No split or trial count is stated.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Compares standard accuracy as training-set size varies for models trained against an ℓ2-bounded adversary; corresponding ℓ∞ results are in Appendix G. No split or trial count is stated.

datasets.name: Restricted ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Compares standard accuracy as training-set size varies for models trained against an ℓ2-bounded adversary; corresponding ℓ∞ results are in Appendix G. No split or trial count is stated.

metrics.name: Standard accuracy
metrics.caveat: Does not indicate adversarial robustness; the paper reports adversarial accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: Adversarial accuracy
metrics.caveat: Does not indicate standard accuracy; the paper reports standard accuracy alongside it.

controls.name: Standard training (ε_train = 0) reference model
controls.detail: An unmodified, non-adversarially-trained classifier is compared with adversarially trained models.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the reported accuracy or representation differences are associated with adversarial training rather than being present in the standard-training reference condition.

confounds.name: The accuracy–robustness trade-off is an artifact of the adversarial-training method
confounds.detail: The observed standard-accuracy reduction could arise from the training procedure rather than an inherent incompatibility between standard accuracy and robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Proves a standard-versus-robust accuracy trade-off for the specified data distribution, including in the distribution-level setting, rather than attributing the result only to an empirical training method.

confounds.name: The trade-off is caused only by insufficient training data
confounds.detail: The apparent loss in standard accuracy could be a finite-sample effect rather than a trade-off that persists with ample data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Shows standard accuracy declining relative to the standard model as training data increase, and proves a trade-off for the specified distribution-level classification problem.

confounds.name: Robust models' behavior is due to gradient obfuscation
confounds.detail: Adversarial examples or apparent robustness could be artifacts of gradients that are ill-suited to first-order attacks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Applies PGD to robust models and shows the resulting large-ε examples change in meaningful, salient ways and can resemble another class, providing evidence against gradient obfuscation.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses a subset of 1,000 samples from the test set. Evaluates ℓ∞ with ε=8/255 and ℓ2 with ε=0.5 on M1–M3; M4 is evaluated only with ℓ∞. Reports attack success rate as the fraction of samples for which an adversarial example is found. No preprocessing is specified.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: ASR does not reflect computational cost; the paper reports queries and execution time alongside it.

controls.name: Attack-sequence ablations
controls.detail: Runs APGD-CE alone, APGD-CE+APGD-T, then adds FAB-T and SQUARE Attack in sequence.
controls.rules_out: Whether later attacks contribute additional ASR beyond earlier attacks, and whether any gain justifies their added computational cost.

controls.name: Random initialization disabled
controls.detail: Runs the attack configurations without random initialization and compares them with configurations where it is enabled.
controls.rules_out: Whether observed results require random initialization.

controls.name: EoT disabled
controls.detail: Runs configurations without Expectation over Transformation and compares them with configurations where it is applied.
controls.rules_out: Whether observed results require EoT.

evidence_standards.name: One fixed seed; no uncertainty or significance procedure reported
evidence_standards.detail: The experiments use a fixed seed for reproducibility. The paper reports point estimates, but gives no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical test. It describes ASR changes typically at or below 0.1 percentage points as negligible, not as a formal significance threshold.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses ResNeXt-34 (2x32) networks. Attacks 1000 randomly selected images in both the ℓ2 and ℓ∞ norms using Carlini–Wagner, Boundary, LogBarrier, and PGD attacks; reports the best adversarial distance per image and error at specified distances. Reports clean Top-1 error. The paper does not specify the evaluation split or evaluation preprocessing.

datasets.name: ImageNet-1k
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses ResNet-50 networks. Attacks 1000 randomly selected images in both the ℓ2 and ℓ∞ norms using Carlini–Wagner, Boundary, LogBarrier, and PGD attacks; reports the best adversarial distance per image and error at specified distances. Reports clean Top-5 error. The paper does not specify the evaluation split or evaluation preprocessing.

baselines.name: Undefended network
baselines.fair_comparison: The CIFAR-10 conditions use ResNeXt-34 (2x32), and the ImageNet-1k conditions use ResNet-50. CIFAR-10 networks are trained with standard data augmentation and learning-rate schedules; the paper does not give further matching details.

baselines.name: 7-step ℓ∞ adversarial training, ε = 2/255
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 using the same network architecture as the regularized models; uses the hyperparameters in Madry et al. (2017), with 7 steps of FGSM projected onto an ℓ∞ ball of radius 2/255.

baselines.name: 7-step ℓ∞ adversarial training, ε = 8/255
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 using the same network architecture as the regularized models; uses the hyperparameters in Madry et al. (2017), with 7 steps of FGSM projected onto an ℓ∞ ball of radius 8/255.

metrics.name: Clean error (Top-1 on CIFAR-10; Top-5 on ImageNet-1k)
metrics.caveat: Clean error alone does not measure adversarial robustness; the paper reports adversarial errors and robustness distances alongside it.

metrics.name: Adversarial error at specified perturbation distances
metrics.caveat: PGD does not find the closest adversarial example for every image; the paper reports results using the best adversarial distance per image across the attack suite, including gradient-free and non-local attacks.

metrics.name: Mean empirical adversarial distance
metrics.caveat: A gradient-based attack alone can give a false impression of robustness; the paper takes the best per-image distance across Carlini–Wagner, Boundary, LogBarrier, and PGD attacks.

metrics.name: L-bound
metrics.caveat: The reported L-bound was vacuous in the ℓ∞ results, giving an upper bound of 100% test error at all distances; the paper reports ω-bound and empirical attack results alongside it.

metrics.name: ω-bound
metrics.caveat: This is a heuristic because L and ω are estimated, and the estimate of ω can fail on some test images. The paper compares it with empirical attack results and reports that it is closer to empirical results than the L-bound.

metrics.name: Estimated loss-gradient norms and modulus of continuity ω(ε)
metrics.caveat: These quantities are estimates rather than exact values; the paper reports them alongside empirical attacks and robustness bounds.

metrics.name: Randomized-smoothing robustness bound
metrics.caveat: The paper describes this as a tight, exact bound and uses it to check its heuristic robustness measures; it is reported alongside those measures.

controls.name: Undefended network
controls.detail: A network trained without the paper's gradient regularization, evaluated on the same datasets and with the same attack suite.
controls.rules_out: That the reported robustness is merely the performance of the underlying architecture and ordinary training without the intervention.

confounds.name: Gradient masking or obfuscation makes gradient-based attacks fail without genuine robustness
confounds.detail: Small or hidden gradients could make PGD ineffective and produce an apparent robustness gain even if adversarial examples remain nearby.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates with the gradient-free Boundary attack and non-local LogBarrier attack, as well as Carlini–Wagner and PGD, and uses robustness certification bounds including randomized smoothing.

confounds.name: Small local gradients conceal rapid loss changes nearby
confounds.detail: For nonsmooth networks, a small gradient at the input does not ensure the loss remains small nearby; first-order approximation error could leave the model vulnerable despite gradient regularization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Estimates the modulus of continuity ω(ε), reports ω-bound results, and compares bounds with empirical adversarial distances obtained from the attack suite.

datasets.name: ImageNet-1k
datasets.eval_protocol: Clean accuracy is evaluated on the entire test set; robust accuracy is evaluated on adversarial examples generated from 1,000 test samples. PGD uses 40 steps and ε ∈ {0.001, 0.003, 0.005, 0.01}; AutoAttack uses the same radii. Transfer attacks use FGSM with ℓ∞ perturbations up to 0.1. Certified accuracy is reported across radii using denoised randomized smoothing with σ=0.25. The frequency study uses 40-step PGD with low-pass, high-pass, or full-pass filtering.

metrics.name: Robust Accuracy (RA)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that robustness results could be misleading if attacks are insufficiently optimized or gradients are obfuscated; it also reports AutoAttack and transfer-attack results as checks alongside PGD.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness is caused by obfuscated gradients
confounds.detail: A model may appear robust to white-box attacks because gradients do not yield effective adversarial examples, rather than because it is genuinely robust.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses transfer attacks and describes them as a sanity check for detecting obfuscated gradients.

confounds.name: The robustness advantage results from insufficient attack optimization
confounds.detail: A weakly optimized attack could leave models incorrectly appearing robust.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says Appendix A conducts a sanity check to verify that ViT's improvement is not caused by insufficient attack optimization; the supplied text does not specify the measurement.

confounds.name: The robustness comparison is explained by large-scale clean pretraining
confounds.detail: The apparent architecture-related robustness advantage could instead come from models having been pretrained on larger datasets.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It compares ImageNet-fine-tuned CNN checkpoints pretrained on YFCC100M and IG-1B-Targeted with CNNs trained from scratch on ImageNet, and reports that the pretrained CNNs have similar or lower RA.

datasets.name: iNaturalist-H
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the validation set for ablations and model selection and the test set for the main results; reports adversarial accuracy and Average Mistake. Main hierarchical-attack evaluations use 50 iterations at each target height, with perturbation budgets ε∈{4/255, 6/255, 8/255}; adversaries are computed for correctly classified instances. Inputs are projected into the ε-ball around the image and [0,1] image range. The paper reports 42,140 validation and 42,756 test images.

baselines.name: FAT without CHAT (standard adversarial training)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper selects vanilla and CHAT-enhanced models by best PGD50 robustness on the validation set; both use the same ResNet-18/ImageNet-pretrained setup and search the stated m and α grids for each ε.

baselines.name: TRADES without CHAT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with CHAT-enhanced TRADES at the same ε; the paper reports the selected α and iteration settings for each condition and uses β=6.

baselines.name: Standard PGD
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as the conventional attack comparison; the paper reports PGD50 for robustness evaluation and compares attack iteration counts on the same vanilla cross-entropy ResNet-18.

baselines.name: AutoAttack
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as the basis for the paper's NHA-enhanced hierarchical AutoAttack comparison; the reported comparison is between standard and CHAT-enhanced models at the same ε.

baselines.name: Vanilla ResNet-18 trained with Cross-Entropy
baselines.fair_comparison: Used to assess PGD iteration counts; the paper reports PGD5, PGD10, PGD50, and PGD100 on this model.

metrics.name: Robust Accuracy (Accuracy under attack)
metrics.caveat: Does not indicate the semantic severity of a misclassification; the paper reports Average Mistake alongside it.

metrics.name: Average Mistake (AM)
metrics.caveat: Measures hierarchical distance for misclassified instances, but the paper notes that its reported AM can include instances that were already erroneous before perturbation; it also reports Flipped Average Mistake for attack-success cases in the attack trade-off analysis.

metrics.name: Accuracy Drop
metrics.caveat: Measures attack effectiveness but not the semantic severity of successful errors; the paper plots it alongside Flipped Average Mistake.

metrics.name: Flipped Average Mistake
metrics.caveat: Restricts severity to instances whose attack succeeded, but does not by itself show how often the attack succeeds; the paper reports it alongside Accuracy Drop.

controls.name: Standard FAT without curriculum
controls.detail: Adversarial training without CHAT, compared alongside CHAT-enhanced FAT.
controls.rules_out: That the reported gains require only adversarial training, rather than the added curriculum.

controls.name: Scratch initialization at curriculum stages
controls.detail: Uses the curriculum but initializes the new classifier from scratch instead of transferring parent-node weights to children.
controls.rules_out: That the CHAT gain over a curriculum alone is explained by hierarchical stages without the proposed weight-transfer warm-up.

controls.name: Linear curriculum spacing
controls.detail: Uses linear rather than the proposed exponential-like allocation of training iterations across curriculum stages.
controls.rules_out: That the result is independent of how training iterations are allocated across hierarchy levels.

confounds.name: CHAT gains could be due to more adversarial-example replay iterations rather than the curriculum
confounds.detail: The paper notes that its selected curriculum-enhanced models used a higher m than the corresponding standard models and says this could increase the performance gap.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The fixed-setting ablation in Table 3 compares Standard, Scratch, and CHAT with ε=4, α=2, and m=8; CHAT still outperforms Standard and Scratch. The paper does not report a broader matched-m study.

evidence_standards.name: PGD iteration-convergence check
evidence_standards.detail: On a vanilla cross-entropy ResNet-18, PGD50 gives 11.07 accuracy and 3.25 AM, versus 11.06 accuracy and 3.25 AM for PGD100; the paper therefore uses PGD50 for robustness evaluations.

evidence_standards.name: Reported attack and model-selection settings
