metrics.name: Conditional attack success rate (cASR)
metrics.caveat: Ordinary ASR can count failures caused by occlusion, while subtraction-based flooring can underestimate attack effects when the gray patch itself causes many failures. The paper instead reports cASR only on images localized under the matched gray occluder.

metrics.name: Omission, substitution, and displacement rates
metrics.caveat: A single success rate shows failure frequency but collapses distinct failure modes. The paper reports the three-way partition alongside cASR; omission means no box, substitution a box on the patch, and displacement a box on neither target nor patch.

controls.name: Matched gray digital occluder
controls.detail: Evaluate each model with a gray patch in place of the adversarial patch and form the set of images it localizes correctly under that condition.
controls.rules_out: That failures counted by cASR are merely caused by occluding the target or by the model’s baseline localization error.

controls.name: No-patch clean condition
controls.detail: Measure localization accuracy with no patch applied, using IoU ≥ 0.5 as the correctness criterion.
controls.rules_out: That apparent vulnerability is simply due to poor clean-image localization; it also provides a clean reference alongside the gray-occluder control.

confounds.name: The patch’s effect is just target occlusion
confounds.detail: A gray patch covering the target could itself cause detections to fail, producing an apparent adversarial success without an adversarial effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compute cASR only over images the model localizes correctly under the matched gray occluder.

confounds.name: Failures reflect baseline localization errors rather than the attack
confounds.detail: A model might already fail to localize a person even without an effective adversarial patch.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report clean localization and condition cASR on successful localization under the gray occluder.

confounds.name: Digitally simulated patches may not work when physically printed and camera-captured
confounds.detail: The reported attacks are digitally applied, so the headline effect may not transfer to a physical patch in a real camera setting.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors state that no printed patch or camera capture was evaluated.

confounds.name: White-box access may be necessary for the reported attack effect
confounds.detail: The attacks use full access to each model, unlike many real deployments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors state that they use only white-box attacks and leave black-box evaluation to future work.

evidence_standards.name: Evaluation operating points and VLM decoding
evidence_standards.detail: VLMs are decoded greedily with no temperature; closed-set detectors use confidence threshold 0.5 and open-vocabulary detectors 0.3. The default IoU threshold is 0.5, with an additional IoU-threshold sweep discussed in the paper. No seeds, uncertainty intervals, statistical tests, or numerical tie margin are specified.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports natural accuracy and robust accuracy under attacks. PGD uses 20 or 1,000 steps, with ε=0.031 and step size 0.003 for ℓ∞, or ε=0.5 and step size 0.1 for ℓ₂. CW∞ uses ε=0.031 and 100 iterations. SPSA uses ε=0.031, 20 iterations, and 32 samples. The paper does not specify the evaluation split or preprocessing.

baselines.name: ResNet10-TRADES (1/λ=1.0)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared at matching channel widths (32 or 64) on CIFAR-10; the paper gives common training settings of 350 epochs, batch size 100, and SGD with momentum 0.9, and specifies TRADES training with ℓ∞ ε=0.031, step size 0.007, and 10 iterations.

baselines.name: ResNet10-TRADES (1/λ=6.0)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared at matching channel widths (32 or 64) on CIFAR-10; the paper gives common training settings of 350 epochs, batch size 100, and SGD with momentum 0.9, and specifies TRADES training with ℓ∞ ε=0.031, step size 0.007, and 10 iterations.

baselines.name: ODENet
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with SOBlock under the same listed solver choices and solver tolerances in the solver study; no further matching details are stated.

metrics.name: Robust accuracy (A_rob) under PGD
metrics.caveat: PGD robustness can be misleading because adaptive ODE solver step sizes mask gradients; the paper also reports PGD-1,000 and evaluates with CW∞ and gradient-free SPSA, under which the proposed models are much less robust.

controls.name: Fixed-step ODE solvers (Euler and RK4)
controls.detail: The paper compares SOBlock using fixed-step solvers (h=1) with adaptive-step solvers under PGD attacks.
controls.rules_out: The comparison shows that the reported PGD robustness is not explained by the stabilized ODE architecture alone; it occurs with adaptive-step solvers, while fixed-step versions fail under PGD.

controls.name: ODENet without skew-symmetric stabilization
controls.detail: The paper repeats solver comparisons with traditional ODENet, which does not use the proposed skew-symmetric stabilization.
controls.rules_out: Comparing it with SOBlock tests whether PGD robustness depends on the stabilization or also appears with adaptive-step ODE solvers without it.

controls.name: DOPRI5 tolerance variations
controls.detail: The paper varies DOPRI5 tolerance (0.1, 0.01, and 0.001) and measures PGD accuracy and the resulting adaptive steps.
controls.rules_out: The comparison tests whether observed PGD robustness tracks adaptive-step perturbations and solver tolerance, rather than being a fixed property of the architecture.

confounds.name: PGD robustness is caused by gradient masking from adaptive solver step sizes, not genuine adversarial robustness
confounds.detail: The headline PGD robust accuracy could be high because adaptive numerical integration perturbs loss gradients and defeats gradient-based PGD, even if the models remain vulnerable to other attacks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates with CW∞ and gradient-free SPSA and finds the proposed models vulnerable; it also compares adaptive and fixed-step solvers, varies DOPRI5 tolerance, and measures adaptive steps. These measurements support gradient masking rather than ruling it out.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: For white-box attacks, evaluate top-1 accuracy on the 50,000 validation images perturbed by targeted PGD; choose the target class uniformly at random and score accuracy regardless of the target. Use an L∞ perturbation bound ε=16 on a pixel scale of 256, random initialization within the allowed ε cube, and 10–2,000 attack iterations (step size 1, except 1.6 for 10 iterations). For the CAAD black-box evaluation, use the five strongest CAAD 2017 attackers with ε=32 and the all-or-nothing rule: an image counts as correct only if classified correctly under every attacker’s adversarial versions. Clean-image evaluations also use the validation set and report top-1 accuracy.

datasets.name: CAAD 2018 secret ImageNet-like test dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Test against 48 unknown attackers with ε=32 using the all-or-nothing criterion: an image counts as correct only if classified correctly against all attackers. The reported winning entry uses single-crop, single-model testing.

baselines.name: Adversarially trained ResNet-101 and ResNet-152 baselines
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper's baselines use its adversarial-training implementation; denoising comparisons add blocks to the ResNet-152 baseline and evaluate under the same attack protocols.

baselines.name: ALP [10] (Inception-v3)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the 10-iteration PGD ImageNet protocol. The paper cautions this is a system-level comparison because the backbone and implementation differ.

baselines.name: CAAD 2017 winner [15]
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared in the CAAD black-box evaluation using the CAAD 2018 all-or-nothing criterion; the paper also reports its result with the two attackers it is most vulnerable to removed.

metrics.name: CAAD all-or-nothing accuracy
metrics.caveat: The score requires correct classification under every attacker's adversarial versions, making it a particularly strict criterion. The paper also reports the CAAD 2017 winner's score after excluding the two attackers it is most vulnerable to.

controls.name: Adversarially trained ResNet-152 baseline without denoising blocks
controls.detail: The reference ResNet-152 is trained with the same adversarial-training implementation as the denoising models.
controls.rules_out: That the denoising result is explained solely by the adversarial-training procedure.

controls.name: Null denoising blocks (1×1 convolution only)
controls.detail: Add four blocks containing the 1×1 convolution and residual connection but no denoising operation; the dot-product non-local and local-filter versions have the same number of extra parameters.
controls.rules_out: That the improvement is due merely to adding parameters or the block's 1×1 convolution.

controls.name: Four standard bottleneck blocks
controls.detail: Add four standard bottleneck blocks to the ResNet-152 baseline (ResNet-164).
controls.rules_out: That the denoising result is explained just by adding network depth or capacity.

controls.name: Denoising-block ablations removing the 1×1 convolution or residual connection
controls.detail: Evaluate the Gaussian non-local blocks with either component removed; removing the residual connection also causes training not to converge.
controls.rules_out: That the 1×1 convolution or residual connection is unnecessary to the denoising block's effect.

controls.name: Clean-trained models and clean-image evaluation
controls.detail: Evaluate clean-trained baseline and denoising models on clean ImageNet validation images, and also report clean-image accuracy for adversarially trained models.
controls.rules_out: That the adversarial robustness result simply reflects a general improvement in clean-image accuracy.

confounds.name: The gains come from extra parameters or model capacity rather than denoising
confounds.detail: Adding parameters or depth could improve accuracy even if feature denoising itself has no effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against parameter-matched null blocks and four added standard bottleneck blocks; the denoising variants perform better in the reported white-box ablation.

confounds.name: The gains are due to adversarial training alone
confounds.detail: A strong adversarial-training implementation could explain the observed robustness without a contribution from denoising.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare denoising models with ResNet baselines trained using the same adversarial-training implementation and evaluate them under the same attack protocols.

confounds.name: The result is a clean-accuracy gain rather than an adversarial-robustness-specific effect
confounds.detail: A general improvement in ordinary classification could produce higher adversarial accuracy without a specific robustness benefit.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate clean-trained models on clean ImageNet images; denoising results are within about ±0.2% of the baseline, and the paper reports the adversarial-versus-clean training tradeoff.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness is caused by the denoising blocks obstructing white-box gradients
confounds.detail: If attackers cannot differentiate through the blocks, apparent robustness might reflect an attack failure rather than defense.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says white-box attackers can back-propagate through the denoising blocks and reports differentiable PGD evaluations extending to 2,000 iterations.

confounds.name: The CAAD 2017 winner's all-or-nothing result reflects vulnerability to only a subset of attackers
confounds.detail: Its aggregate score could conceal that a small number of attackers account for most failures.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports the winner's score after removing the two attackers it is most vulnerable to; it rises from 0.04% to 13.4% under the remaining three.

confounds.name: The observed feature changes quantitatively establish that denoising reduces feature noise
confounds.detail: Changes in feature magnitudes or distributions across architectures and training methods could look like denoising without establishing that feature noise was reduced.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors say it is nontrivial to quantitatively compare feature-noise levels across models and do not provide a quantitative feature-noise measure.

evidence_standards.name: Three independent clean-training runs for the ResNet-152 baseline
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports the baseline's run-to-run accuracy differences as +0.05% and −0.04%; it treats denoising-model differences within about ±0.2% as not significant given this natural variation. No formal statistical test is specified.

evidence_standards.name: CAAD 2018 winning-entry test setting
evidence_standards.detail: The reported 50.6% result uses single-crop, single-model testing. The paper does not state repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or a statistical test for this result.

datasets.name: CIFAR
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on 100 samples from the model’s test dataset; robust accuracy is the fraction classified correctly within the perturbation bound ε=8/255. The paper does not specify further preprocessing.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on 100 samples from the model’s test dataset; robust accuracy is the fraction classified correctly within the perturbation bound ε=0.5. The paper does not specify further preprocessing.

baselines.name: PGD
baselines.fair_comparison: Run on the same models and test-sample evaluation protocol; perturbation bounds are ε=8/255 for CIFAR models and ε=0.5 for MNIST models. Step size matches the original evaluations, while patched runs may change attack settings.

baselines.name: APGDCE (AutoPGD with Cross-Entropy loss)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same models and test-sample evaluation protocol, using the stated perturbation bound for each model.

baselines.name: APGDDLR (AutoPGD with Difference of Logits Ratio loss)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same models and test-sample evaluation protocol, using the stated perturbation bound for each model.

metrics.name: Robust accuracy (RA)
metrics.caveat: Can overstate robustness when the attack fails because of optimization or implementation problems; the paper reports Indicators of Attack Failure (IoAF) alongside RA.

confounds.name: Gradients are unavailable or numerically unstable, so the attack fails despite adversarial examples being possible
confounds.detail: A high robust-accuracy result could reflect non-differentiable components or numerical instability rather than genuine robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: I1 flags a zero-norm input gradient or a gradient-computation error; the paper applies BPDA to address the failure.

confounds.name: Gradients are stochastic or uninformative, so following them does not reduce the loss
confounds.detail: A high robust-accuracy result could arise from noisy loss landscapes or randomized inference defeating the attack optimization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: I2 measures relative loss variability on perturbed inputs; the paper uses EoT when this indicator detects instability.

confounds.name: The attack discards adversarial examples found before its final step
confounds.detail: The reported robustness could be high because the implementation returns a non-adversarial final point despite having found an adversarial point along the attack path.
confounds.ruled_out_by: I3 checks whether the final point is non-adversarial while an earlier point in the path is adversarial.

confounds.name: The attack has not converged because its iteration count or step size is inadequate
confounds.detail: A high robust-accuracy result could be caused by stopping optimization too early or using an unsuitable step size.
confounds.ruled_out_by: I4 tracks the cumulative-minimum loss curve and flags insufficient loss decrement in the last k iterations; the paper uses k=10 and a 1% threshold.

confounds.name: The attack is non-adaptive and does not transfer from its surrogate to the defended target
confounds.detail: A high robust-accuracy result could reflect failure to bypass defense components or detectors omitted from the surrogate, rather than robustness to an adaptive attack.
confounds.ruled_out_by: I5 checks whether the attack bypasses the surrogate but not the target.

confounds.name: The attack is trapped in a bad local minimum or otherwise cannot reach a misclassified region
confounds.detail: A high robust-accuracy result could persist because the optimizer cannot find an adversarial example, even without a perturbation bound.
confounds.ruled_out_by: I6 runs an unconstrained attack and flags failure to find an adversarial example.

confounds.name: A stronger or different attack could still reduce the measured robustness even when no indicator triggers
confounds.detail: The authors caution that absence of detected failures does not establish that robustness cannot be worsened by another, more powerful attack.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper explicitly presents this as a limitation of empirical evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: IoAF subset and trigger rules
evidence_standards.detail: I1, I2, and I6 are computed on a random subset of N=10 samples; I1 and I2 are reported if triggered on at least one sample, and I6 is reported if it fails on at least one sample. I2 uses s=100 perturbed inputs, an ℓ2 radius r=10^-3, and threshold τ=10%. I4 uses k=10 final iterations and threshold μ=1%. The paper reports no seed-based uncertainty estimates or statistical significance tests.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Main case study reports robust accuracy against ℓ∞ perturbations, generally ε=8/255; Chen et al. (2021) is evaluated at ε=2/255. The paper reports results on 1,000 test points/images where specified (Shi et al. uses the first 1,000 test images). Attacks are defense-specific; the underlying static model is also evaluated. For Mao et al. (2021), the evaluation uses batch size 50 instead of the original 512.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: AID-purifier evaluation on 1,000 points against ℓ∞ perturbations of ε=8/255; static models are evaluated with AutoAttack and dynamic models with APGD+BPDA.

datasets.name: SVHN
datasets.eval_protocol: AID-purifier evaluation on 1,000 points against ℓ∞ perturbations of ε=12/255; static models are evaluated with AutoAttack and dynamic models with APGD+BPDA.

baselines.name: TRADES classifier (Zhang et al., 2019)
baselines.fair_comparison: SODEF uses the robust TRADES classifier as its feature extractor, without its last linear layer; the paper compares the underlying classifier with SODEF, using AutoAttack for the static model and transferred APGD for SODEF.

baselines.name: Gowal et al. (2020) model
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as the underlying static model and with HD on the same evaluation points; the reported table uses the stated static and transferred-attack conditions.

baselines.name: Carmon et al. (2019) model
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as the underlying static model and with HD on the same evaluation points; the reported table uses the stated static and transferred-attack conditions.

baselines.name: Andriushchenko & Flammarion (2020) model
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as the underlying static model and with HD on the same evaluation points; the reported table uses the stated static and transferred-attack conditions.

baselines.name: Madry et al. (2018) adversarially trained static models
baselines.fair_comparison: AID-purifier is compared with the corresponding static models on the same datasets and points; the paper evaluates static models with AutoAttack and dynamic models with APGD+BPDA.

baselines.name: AWP-pretrained static CIFAR-10 model (Wu et al., 2020a)
baselines.fair_comparison: The two-iteration Alfarra defense is compared with its underlying static model on CIFAR-10 at ε=8/255, including under RayS.

metrics.name: Robust accuracy
metrics.caveat: An unsuccessful or insufficiently adaptive attack can overestimate robustness; AutoAttack may also return clean inputs when it finds no adversarial example or the input is already misclassified, inflating transferred-attack results. The paper reports adaptive attacks on the full defense, and often reports results for the underlying static model alongside.

metrics.name: Inference time relative to the underlying static model
metrics.caveat: The measured multiplier depends on factors including model architecture, compute infrastructure, and implementation; the paper reports runtime observed in its evaluation.

controls.name: Underlying static model without test-time adaptation
controls.detail: The paper reports the robust accuracy of the static classifier underlying each adaptive defense alongside the adaptive version where available.
controls.rules_out: Whether the adaptive intervention improves or weakens the underlying static model under the stated evaluation.

controls.name: Mao et al. defense with randomness removed
controls.detail: The authors fix the random seed and omit EoT when evaluating the adaptive defense; robust accuracy is 56.4%, compared with 58.4% for the evaluation with randomness and EoT.
controls.rules_out: Whether the measured result depends on randomness in the defense.

confounds.name: Weak or non-adaptive attacks make a defense appear robust
confounds.detail: Transfer attacks from the static model may not exploit the adaptive defense; default AutoAttack behavior can also leave clean inputs in the transferred set when it finds no adversarial example or the input is already misclassified.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses adaptive attacks against the full defense, including APGD with BPDA and EoT where appropriate, and uses custom APGD that returns worst-case adversarial examples rather than defaulting to the original input.

confounds.name: Obfuscated or inaccurate gradients conceal vulnerability
confounds.detail: Optimization, projections, or many iterations can make gradients non-differentiable, vanish, or explode, potentially making gradient attacks look ineffective.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper applies BPDA with gradient approximations; for Shi et al. it also averages gradients over intermediate purification iterates.

confounds.name: Randomness, rather than optimization, accounts for a defense's measured effect
confounds.detail: Randomized defenses can yield different outputs for the same input, and an attack that does not account for this may mismeasure robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper uses EoT for randomized defenses and, for Mao et al., also fixes the random seed and removes EoT to measure the result without randomness.

confounds.name: Alfarra defense's confidence flattening or score-based attack difficulty creates apparent robustness without changing the decision boundary
confounds.detail: Increasing confidence in the model's original prediction can flatten the cross-entropy loss landscape and cause score-based attacks to fail, even though the defense inherits the underlying classifier's decision boundary.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates with RayS, a decision-based attack that does not use confidence scores, and obtains the same 66.6% robust accuracy for the defense and static model.

confounds.name: AID-purifier's apparent SVHN gain reflects a weak static-model starting point
confounds.detail: The paper notes that the SVHN static model has low robust accuracy, unlike the CIFAR models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It notes that standard adversarial training can produce a classifier with more than 40% robust and 86% clean accuracy, contextualizing the apparent gain.

confounds.name: Mao et al. evaluation's smaller batch size weakens the defense
confounds.detail: The evaluation uses batch size 50 instead of the original 512, which the authors note may negatively impact the defense.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors check that transfer-attack results with their setup match the reported results: AutoAttack gives 67.0% versus 67.79%, and custom APGD gives 63.9% versus 63.83%.

evidence_standards.name: Five repeated evaluations for ADP, with mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The reported 33.7% robust accuracy is averaged over five repeated evaluations on the adversarially perturbed points, with standard deviation ±0.54%; the paper states no statistical test or threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Robustness evaluation uses the RobustBench interface on 10,000 test instances, with the leaderboard settings ℓ∞, ε=8/255 and ℓ2, ε=0.5; attack ε is set to match the defense. For AE construction, 5,000 randomly selected training instances are used. Transferability experiments use adversarial examples generated from the 10,000 test instances and evaluate transfers among Semi-Adv, LBGAT, and MMA.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Robustness evaluation uses the RobustBench interface on all 10,000 test instances, for ℓ∞, ε=8/255; attack ε is set to match the defense.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Robustness evaluation uses the RobustBench interface on its fixed set of 5,000 test instances, for ℓ∞, ε=4/255; attack ε is set to match the defense.

datasets.name: RobustBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses leaderboard defenses up to January 2022 and the integrated RobustBench evaluation interface: top 15 defenses for CIFAR-10 ℓ∞ (ε=8/255), top 15 for CIFAR-10 ℓ2 (ε=0.5), and top 5 each for CIFAR-100 ℓ∞ (ε=8/255) and ImageNet ℓ∞ (ε=4/255). The paper also includes five additional defenses for which CAA results were available.

baselines.name: AutoAttack
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same RobustBench defenses, test instances, and norm constraints; the paper uses the leaderboard’s reported AutoAttack robust accuracies. AutoAttack remains fixed across defenses, while AutoAE uses a unified ensemble.

baselines.name: CAA (Composite Adversarial Attack)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same RobustBench defenses, test instances, and norm constraints where CAA results are available. CAA builds a separate attack policy for each defense, whereas AutoAE uses a unified ensemble.

confounds.name: AutoAE’s apparent performance could come from tuning to its construction defenses rather than transferring to unseen, stronger defenses
confounds.detail: If the ensemble only worked on the weaker defenses used during construction, its headline robustness evaluations would not establish a useful general evaluation protocol.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Construct AEs using CIFAR-10 adversarial-training models described as weaker or outdated, then evaluate on 45 RobustBench defenses, including previously unseen and stronger models.

confounds.name: Adversarial examples could be defense-specific and fail to transfer between defenses
confounds.detail: If the generated examples only fooled the model they were generated against, the approach would have limited transferability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Transfer adversarial examples among Semi-Adv, LBGAT, and MMA and compare test accuracy across the transfer scenarios.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed random seeds, deterministic model forward passes, and one restart per component attack
evidence_standards.detail: The paper fixes attack random seeds to stabilize outputs, notes that tested defenses have deterministic forward passes, and uses one restart for each component attack. It reports no variance estimates, statistical tests, or numerical margin for declaring differences real.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for certified robustness; also used at σ=1.0 for the accuracy–certified-accuracy trade-off experiment, with certified accuracy evaluated at r=2.0. Certification uses n=100,000, n₀=100, and α=0.001.

datasets.name: Fashion-MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for certified robustness; the text refers to Appendix C for results. Certification uses n=100,000, n₀=100, and α=0.001.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the test set for σ∈{0.25, 0.5, 1.0}, reporting ACR and approximate certified test accuracy over radii. Certification uses n=100,000, n₀=100, and α=0.001.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated for certified robustness; the text refers to Appendix C for results. Certification uses n=100,000, n₀=100, and α=0.001.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated at σ=1.0 on a uniformly subsampled 500 examples from the validation dataset; reports ACR and approximate certified accuracy. Certification uses n=100,000, n₀=100, and α=0.001.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10-C

confounds.name: Corruption-robustness gains come from prior knowledge of the corruptions
confounds.detail: The gains on CIFAR-10-C could reflect training with prior knowledge of the corruption types rather than the proposed training method.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors state that the gains do not come from prior knowledge about multiple corruptions (except Gaussian noise); they evaluate on CIFAR-10-C corruptions and compare against other robust-training methods.

confounds.name: Corruption-robustness gains come merely from using adversarial search during training
confounds.detail: The CIFAR-10-C gains could be due to adversarial search itself rather than CAT-RS’s sample-dependent training objective.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare with SmoothAdv, which also uses adversarial search, and report that it does not improve mAcc on CIFAR-10-C over Gaussian training, whereas CAT-RS does.

evidence_standards.name: Monte Carlo certification settings
evidence_standards.detail: Certify uses n=100,000 samples, n₀=100, and α=0.001; its certified-radius lower bound is returned with probability at least 1−α, or certification abstains.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports clean classification accuracy and adversarial accuracy. Table 1 evaluates ResNet-18 models under 10-step PGD; Table 2 reports AutoAttack accuracy for the ℓ∞ threat model with ε=8/255; Table 3 uses AutoAttack with the same threat model; Table 4 reports AutoAttack for ℓ∞, ε=8/255 and ℓ₂, ε=128/255. Checkpoint selection in Table 2 uses a separate validation set; the paper does not specify a test split or preprocessing.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports clean classification accuracy and AutoAttack accuracy for the ℓ∞ threat model with ε=8/255. Checkpoint split and preprocessing are not specified.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses a FreeAT-trained ResNet-50 to visualize semantic gradients on clean test images; highlights the top 10% of pixel positions by total derivatives across the three RGB channels. No test-set size or preprocessing is specified.

baselines.name: PGD-AT with KL divergence
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the SE version using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 under the same basic training setup and threat model. The KL baseline uses initial learning rate 0.1 versus 0.05 for the SE methods; checkpoints are selected on a separate validation set by PGD-10 accuracy using KL for the baseline and SE for the proposed method.

baselines.name: TRADES with KL divergence
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the SE version using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 under the same basic training setup and threat model, with β=6. The KL baseline uses initial learning rate 0.1 versus 0.05 for the SE methods; checkpoint selection uses PGD-10 validation accuracy with the corresponding loss.

baselines.name: Rebuffi et al. (2021)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on matching listed architecture, dataset, threat model, and 1M DDPM-generated-data setting in the corresponding table rows. The paper's runs use batch size 512 and 400 epochs, versus the baseline's 1024 and 800 epochs; its runs also do not apply CutMix.

controls.name: KL-divergence objective reference
controls.detail: The KL-based PGD-AT and TRADES conditions are compared alongside the SE-based versions in the same basic ResNet-18 setting; the learning rates and validation checkpoint criteria differ as described for the baselines.
controls.rules_out: Provides the paper's reference condition for comparing the SE objective with the usual KL objective within the adversarial-training frameworks.

controls.name: SE without clipping
controls.detail: Table 2 reports SE-based PGD-AT and TRADES both with and without the loss-clipping operation.
controls.rules_out: A difference from the clipped SE condition measures the contribution of clipping, rather than attributing the result to the SE objective alone.

evidence_standards.name: Five runs with mean ± standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: Table 2 averages results over five runs and reports mean ± standard deviation. The paper gives no statistical test, significance threshold, or margin for treating results as equivalent.
